headline: Milford Gulf porgies stack three deep on a green crab, sea bass along for the ride
subhead: The neap tide made the rockpiles easy pickings this week — porgies and sea bass came fast, blackfish took more convincing.
body_markdown:
First drop off the Gulf rocks Tuesday morning, I'm still tying my second hook when the rod loads up. Porgy, a good one, maybe a pound and a half, and he's got two buddies right behind him before I even get the bail closed on the next rig. That's the kind of start that tells you everything about how this week's gone out there — the porgies have been thick and cooperative, and for once I didn't have to work for it.

We flagged this last week — said the softening neap tide would make for easier drift conditions over structure, and that's exactly what played out. Current's been gentle enough that a half-ounce sinker holds bottom in 25 feet without getting swept sideways into the rocks, which around the Gulf and out toward Charles Island is usually a losing battle. Less current means better bait presentation, less snagged rigs, more fish in the box. Simple as that.

The porgy bite has been the story of the week from the Milford breakwalls straight out to the humps off Charles Island. Green crab halves and sandworms on a high-low rig, size 4 to 2 hooks, fishing right on bottom in 18 to 28 feet. Best window's been the last two hours of the incoming into the top of high water — that's when I've seen the marks stack up thick on the sounder over the rockier patches south of the Charles Island bar. Once the tide turns and starts pushing hard the other way, even on this weak neap cycle, the bite tends to shut off fast. So get there early, fish the flood, and don't overstay once it turns.

Sea bass have been mixed in wherever there's real structure — the rockpiles off Falkner Island have been holding some quality fish, several pushing 16 to 18 inches, taken on the same crab baits or a small strip of squid fished tight to the bottom. I've had days out there where it's porgy-sea bass-porgy-sea bass for twenty minutes straight, then it just stops like someone flipped a switch. That's typical mid-summer sea bass behavior on these reefs — they group up tight and then move off the pile, so if the action dies, pick up and move fifty yards rather than sit on dead water.

Blackfish have been tougher. Water's warm enough now — we're seeing upper 60s to low 70s across the western Sound — that the tog have gotten a little lazy and choosy. I managed three keepers off the rockpile structure north of Stratford Shoal on green crab, but it took patience and a lot of missed bites that felt more like nibbles than commitments. If you're set on blackfish this week, I'd fish smaller pieces of crab, keep the bait fresh, and be ready for a long game rather than a fast bite.

Stripers are exactly where you'd expect them in this heat — deep and mostly nocturnal. Daytime trips around the Charles Island sandbar haven't produced much beyond the occasional schoolie chasing bait in the wash at first light. The better fish have slid off into deeper water and gone quiet during daylight, which tracks with what's happening up and down the whole Sound right now. If you want a striper over the summer slot, you need to be out there at dawn working the drop-off on the south side of the bar with a bucktail, or better yet, fish it at night with a swimming plug worked slow over the sandbar structure. I had one solid fish, mid-20s, come off a white bucktail worked along the edge where the bar drops into deeper water just as the sky started to lighten — that's been the pattern, first and last light, nothing consistent in between.

Bluefish have actually been the more dependable daytime target if you want reliable rod-bending action without waiting for dark. There's bait — peanut bunker mostly — showing up along the New Haven Harbor breakwalls and pushing east toward Hammonasset, and the blues have been on them hard during the middle of the day. Nothing subtle about it — cast a metal lure, a Deadly Dick or an Ava jig, into the surface commotion and hang on. It's not the sophisticated structure fishing I love, but if you want steady bent rods with the kids or you just want to burn off some frustration after a slow tog session, that's been the move.

Looking at the week ahead, I expect the porgy and sea bass bite to hold up as long as this gentle current keeps going, though tides will start rebuilding strength over the next several days as we move away from the neap. That'll make drift fishing trickier over the rockpiles — heavier sinkers, more attention to positioning — but it should also start pushing more bait and more aggressive feeding around structure edges. If I had one morning to fish this week, I'd hit the Gulf rocks or the Charles Island humps on the last of an incoming tide, work green crab on bottom, and stay flexible enough to chase sea bass around if the porgies slow down. Blackfish guys, keep your expectations tempered and your bait fresh — this warm stretch isn't doing you any favors, but the fish are still there for those willing to grind it out.
